correction.text: Cai at Shangcai, 'enfeoffed at present-day Shangcai (lit. "Upper Cai") in Henan', until Chu annexed the state in 531 BC; the ledger carries the later seats: Xincai from the restoration of 529 ('first to Xincai (lit. "New Cai") in 531 BC') and Xiacai from 493

keyframe_review.note: 3,683 km2 at 113.06-113.84 E, 34.34-34.92 N: the shape sits around Xuchang and Xinzheng, 120 km north-west of Shangcai (33.262°N 114.264°E per the Shangcai County infobox), inside Zheng's country; Cliopatria's oversized Chu shape (to 34.7 N) covers Shangcai itself, which is why Cai was drawn displaced. The corrected shape is Shangcai alone (35 km, about 3,850 km2, Cliopatria's size) for 750-531; the ledger removes it in 531 (loss to Chu, the whole state), restores Cai at Xincai in 529, and moves it to Xiacai in 493 (loss of Xincai, gain of Xiacai). The first version drew the union of Shangcai and Xincai (about 6,700 km2) for the whole span, so Cai held Xincai from 750 and kept it through the Chu annexation of 531-529 and the 529 gain changed nothing (reviewer finding, 2026-10-18). Annexed by Chu 531-529 (ledger).

correction.text: Xiacai (lit. 'Lower Cai') 'at present-day Fengtai County in Anhui', valid to 447 BC

keyframe_review.note: The same misplaced shape for 480-451. By 480 Cai had moved 'to Xiacai (lit. "Lower Cai") at present-day Fengtai County in Anhui' (493 BC in the usual accounts), on the Huai 250 km east of the drawn shape, and the state ended in 447 ('Conquered by Chu: 447 bce'), not 451.

ledger.note: c. 1045: Cai Shu Du enfeoffed at Shangcai. 'Following his overthrow of the Shang king Zhou, King Wu of Zhou granted titles and territories to his younger brothers. The fifth brother, Cai Shu Du, was enfeoffed at present-day Shangcai (lit. "Upper Cai") in Henan'; infobox 'Established: c. 1045 bce'. Cai Shu Du was exiled after the Three Guards Rebellion and his son Ji Hu was rewarded 'with the reestablishment of his father's territory and title' (undated).
531: King Ling of Chu seizes Cai. 'In 531 BC, King Ling tricked and captured Marquis Ling of Cai, blamed him for killing his own father'; Qiji 'was made Duke of Cai'. The whole state becomes Chu's.

531: the seat moves to Xincai. 'Invasions from Chu ... relocated Cai several times, first to Xincai (lit. "New Cai") in 531 BC'. In the usual accounts the move belongs to the restoration of 529 (King Ping of Chu); the page's year is kept.

529: Cai restored at Xincai. Not dated on the pages opened: the King Ling page ends with his suicide in 'winter 529 BC' and the Cai page's ruler list resumes with 'Marquis Ping of Cai: 530–522 BC'. Confidence 1; the usual account is King Ping of Chu's restoration of Cai and Chen in 529. The King Ping of Chu page (opened 2026-10-18) is silent on the restoration, and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_Ping_of_Cai does not exist (URL not found).

493: the seat moves to Xiacai (Zhoulai). 'later to Xiacai (lit. "Lower Cai") at present-day Fengtai County in Anhui'; the page gives no year, and the Marquis Zhao of Cai page would not load, so 493 BC is the researcher's, confidence 1. The King Zhao of Chu page (opened 2026-10-18) is also silent on Cai, so the year stays the researcher's.

region.text: Cai at Xincai (lit. 'New Cai'), left for Xiacai

ledger.note: 493: Cai gives up Xincai. 'later to Xiacai (lit. "Lower Cai") at present-day Fengtai County in Anhui' (Cai page, no year; 493 is the researcher's, as for the move itself). The land at Xincai goes to Chu (the Chu dossier's 493 gain); without this entry Cai would hold Xincai until the cai_-480 keyframe takes over 13 years after the seat moved (reviewer finding, 2026-10-18). Confidence 1: the year and the taker rest on no page.

ledger.note: 493: Cai takes Xiacai. 'later to Xiacai (lit. "Lower Cai") at present-day Fengtai County in Anhui' (Cai page, no year). The pages opened do not say who held the land at Fengtai, so the counterpart is 'nobody'; drawn as 30 km at gazetteer place Huainan (Fengtai is 20 km north-west of it), the same circle as the cai_-480 keyframe and the 447 dissolve. Confidence 1, like the move.

'In 447 BC, King Hui of Chu conquered Cai completely, but allowed the marquesses to settle near Changde in Hunan and establish a rump state called Gaocai. This was destroyed 80 years later.' Infobox 'Conquered by Chu: 447 bce'; the Chu page: 'overran Cai to the north in 447 BC'. Cliopatria keeps Cai to 451.

notes:
Cliopatria rows to correct: both Cai shapes are misplaced 120 km north-west of Shangcai (verified against the Shangcai County coordinates), the second should be at Xiacai (Fengtai, on the Huai), and the row should end 447, not 451; the displacement comes from Cliopatria's oversized early Chu shape, which covers Shangcai (see the Chu dossier). Page that would not load: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_Zhao_of_Cai (URL not found, retried); so the 493 move to Xiacai (Zhoulai), the Chu siege of 494 and Cai's detention episode (509-506) rest on no page and the move is at confidence 1. The 529 restoration is inferred from the ruler lists (confidence 1). Gazetteer names needed: Shangcai (place, 33.262 N 114.264 E), Xincai (place, Xincai County, Zhumadian, c. 32.75 N 114.98 E), Fengtai/Xiacai (place, Fengtai County, Huainan, c. 32.71 N 116.72 E; the dossier uses gazetteer place Huainan with a 30 km radius instead). The Gaocai rump near Changde (447 to c. 367) is a Chu-granted enclave and is not drawn.

Repair pass (2026-10-18, after the reviewer's fail): cai_-750 is now Shangcai alone and the ledger carries the later seats (531 loss of Shangcai, 529 gain of Xincai, 493 loss of Xincai and gain of Xiacai), so Cai no longer holds Xincai before it moved there or through the Chu annexation. Between 531 and 529 Cai has no land but the capital dot is at Xincai from 531, the Cai page's year (the usual accounts put the move at the 529 restoration). The 493 loss and gain are bridges at confidence 1 (no page gives the year or says who held Fengtai); the Chu dossier mirrors the loss as its 493 gain of Xincai. Pages opened and silent on Cai: King Zhao of Chu, King Ping of Chu. Page that does not exist: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_Ping_of_Cai (URL not found). The Xiacai circle (Huainan 30) overlaps Chu's Hefei 80 circle (601) by about 500 km2, a radius artefact.
